abstract: |
  Declining body size has been widely hypothesized as a general ecological response of endotherms to anthropogenic climate warming. In tropical biomes, empirical evaluations of multi-decadal phenotypic trends remain scarce. Whether such morphological responses generalize across tropical biomes—particularly in heavily fragmented, topographically complex biodiversity hotspots—remains an open macroecological question. Here, we analyze 24 years (1995–2018) of morphological data from 73 passerine species (12,571 live-capture records; ATLANTIC BIRD TRAITS) across the Brazilian Atlantic Forest to evaluate temporal trajectories in body mass, wing length, bill width, and among-individual variability under 0.25°C/decade of regional warming. Overall, we found little evidence of directional change in body mass (−0.91%/decade, 95% CI: −2.72 to +0.94%). The community-level wing-length trajectory was weakly negative, with a confidence interval overlapping zero (−0.74 mm/decade, 95% CI: −1.55 to +0.07 mm/decade). Interspecific variation is pronounced: while 49 species display negative point estimates, 61 of 72 species with wing data have intervals overlapping zero, indicating community-wide heterogeneity rather than uniform shrinkage. Bill width showed little temporal change (−0.03 mm/decade, 95% CI: −0.18 to +0.13 mm/decade), giving little evidence of the appendage enlargement expected under Allen-type thermoregulatory predictions. On 7,577 shared records from the same individuals, body mass was more conserved than expected under cubic geometric shrinkage (+4.85%/decade contrast, 95% CI: +0.81 to +8.89%), rejecting strict geometric isometry and indicating decoupling between mass and wing length. This departure was robust to the full adjustment set, but was not associated with interannual temperature anomalies, so we do not attribute it to thermal variation. Our findings indicate that passerines in the fragmented Atlantic Forest have displayed only subtle phenotypic changes under warming.
plain-language-summary: |
  As global temperatures rise, many animals are suspected to be shrinking in body size or changing shape to cope with heat. While birds in the intact Amazon rainforest were recently found to be losing weight and growing longer wings over the past four decades, whether birds in other tropical forests respond similarly has been unclear. Examining 24 years of field data (1995–2018) on 73 songbird species across the Brazilian Atlantic Forest, we find no clear evidence that body mass has changed, while wing length shows subtle, species-specific adjustments rather than uniform shrinking. Bills show no sign of enlargement, and body mass was conserved rather than falling in step with the small changes in wing length. Atlantic Forest birds therefore appear to have changed little in size despite significant regional warming, in contrast to patterns reported from the Amazon. By carefully accounting for differences among the research groups that collected the data, and among field sites and seasons, our study offers a macroecological picture of bird responses to climate change in a fragmented tropical landscape.

# format a count with a thousands separator for inline use
.n <- function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE)
# format a signed estimate / CI bound to 2 dp with a true minus sign
.s <- function(x) sub("-", "−", sprintf("%.2f", x))
# format a signed value to 1 dp with a true minus sign
.s1 <- function(x) sub("-", "−", sprintf("%.1f", x))
# format a signed estimate to 4 dp with a true minus sign
.s4 <- function(x) sub("-", "−", sprintf("%.4f", x))
# format a p-value for inline use
.rp <- function(p) if (p < 0.001) "< 0.001" else paste("=", sprintf("%.3f", p))

# pull row from cw_phylo$before_after with optional term filtering
.cw <- function(mod, term = NULL) {
  r <- cw_phylo$before_after[cw_phylo$before_after$model == mod, ]
  if (!is.null(term)) r <- r[r$term == term, ]
  if (nrow(r) == 0) return(list(b = "NA", lo = "NA", hi = "NA", dec = "NA", dec_lo = "NA", dec_hi = "NA", n = "NA"))
  list(
    b      = .s(r$estimate[1]),
    lo     = .s(r$ci_lo[1]),
    hi     = .s(r$ci_hi[1]),
    dec    = .s1(r$mm_per_decade[1]),
    dec_lo = .s1(r$mm_per_decade_lo[1]),
    dec_hi = .s1(r$mm_per_decade_hi[1]),
    n      = .n(r$N[1])
  )
}

.mt_phylo <- function(trait_name, mod, term = "scaled_yr") {
  df <- multi_phylo$comparison_lme4
  r <- df[df$trait == trait_name & df$model == mod & df$term == term, ]
  if (nrow(r) == 0) return(list(b = "NA", b2 = "NA", lo = "NA", hi = "NA", lo2 = "NA", hi2 = "NA", pct = "NA", pct_lo = "NA", pct_hi = "NA", n = "NA"))
  list(
    b      = .s4(r$phylo_estimate[1]),
    b2     = .s(r$phylo_estimate[1]),
    lo     = .s4(r$phylo_lower[1]),
    hi     = .s4(r$phylo_upper[1]),
    lo2    = .s(r$phylo_lower[1]),
    hi2    = .s(r$phylo_upper[1]),
    pct    = .s1(r$phylo_pct_per_decade[1]),
    pct_lo = .s1(r$phylo_pct_lower[1]),
    pct_hi = .s1(r$phylo_pct_upper[1]),
    n      = .n(r$phylo_n[1])
  )
}

# Every number quoted from these blocks is pulled from the saved object, never
# typed into the text.
.rr_row <- function(tbl, ...) {
  f <- list(...); keep <- rep(TRUE, nrow(tbl))
  for (nm in names(f)) keep <- keep & tbl[[nm]] == f[[nm]]
  r <- tbl[keep, , drop = FALSE]
  stopifnot(nrow(r) == 1L)
  r
}
# thermal-anomaly effects (E1-E3)
rr_therm <- function(model, response, term = "dT", tbl = NULL) {
  tb <- if (is.null(tbl)) rr$E3 else tbl
  r <- .rr_row(tb, model = model, response = response, term = term)
  list(z = .s(r$z), p = .rp(r$p), b = .s4(r$estimate), se = sprintf("%.4f", r$se),
       lo = .s4(r$lower), hi = .s4(r$upper), trees = r$trees_used)
}

rr_iso <- function(model) {
  r <- .rr_row(rr$E4, model = model, response = "isometry contrast lnM-3lnL")
  list(pct = .s1(r$pct_decade), lo = .s1(r$pct_decade_lo), hi = .s1(r$pct_decade_hi),
       z = .s(r$z), p = .rp(r$p))
}

       lo = .s1(r$pct_lo), hi = .s1(r$pct_hi),
       t = .s(r$t), b = .s(r$estimate), n = .n(r$n))
}

# Introduction

Climate warming can alter animal morphology through several pathways: direct thermoregulatory selection, changes in resource availability, and developmental or evolutionary responses to a shifting environment [@gardner_declining_2011; @sheridan_shrinking_2011; @teplitsky_climate_2014]. These mechanisms have generated prominent predictions, most familiarly that endotherms should become smaller in warmer environments, because a higher surface-area-to-volume ratio aids metabolic heat dissipation [Bergmann's rule; @bergmann1847; @mayr1956; @ashton2002a], and that heat-dissipating extremities such as bills should enlarge [Allen's rule; @allen1877; @ryding2021shape]. Empirical support for such general responses is, however, mixed. Broad syntheses indicate that morphological responses to contemporary warming vary substantially among traits, species, and ecological contexts rather than following a single directional pattern; @radchuk2019adaptive, synthesising phenotypic responses across wild populations, recovered no consistent systematic morphological response to warming. Understanding this heterogeneity requires determining whether the patterns documented in well-studied systems extend to ecological and geographic settings that remain poorly represented in long-term datasets.

That evidence base is strongly skewed. Multi-decadal morphological analyses have predominantly drawn on temperate, often migratory, bird species sampled through museum collections or long-term ringing stations in the Northern Hemisphere [e.g., @weeks2020], and the synthesis of @radchuk2019adaptive documents the same geographic bias. Tropical communities, where avian diversity peaks, are far less represented, so it remains unclear how general the reported patterns are. Against this background, @jirinec2021morphological provides a valuable tropical benchmark: analysing four decades (1979–2019) of standardized field measurements from 77 non-migratory understorey species in the continuous primary rainforest of the central Amazon (Biological Dynamics of Forest Fragments Project, BDFFP), they documented widespread declines in body mass alongside wing elongation in roughly a third of species, and interpreted the resulting reduction in wing loading as an adaptive shift toward flight economy in an increasingly warm understorey. Whether that pronounced Amazonian response is representative of tropical forest birds more broadly, or is instead strongly context dependent, is the question we address here.

The Brazilian Atlantic Forest offers an informative contrast. It is a global biodiversity hotspot that differs from the continuous lowland central Amazon in almost every respect that might matter: it spans steep topographic and latitudinal gradients, and it has lost over 80% of its original forest cover, leaving the remainder divided among thousands of small, isolated fragments [@ribeiro2009atlantic]. It is therefore a useful test of whether the Amazonian pattern generalizes to a tropical forest system with a very different landscape and thermal structure. We return in the Discussion to the mechanisms that might explain any difference we find.

Two further axes help characterize whatever response is present. First, warming may act on phenotypic variance as well as on trait means, either widening among-individual variation through developmental instability or relaxed selection, or narrowing it through directional canalization [@teplitsky_climate_2014; @debat2001mapping; @badyaev2005stress]. Second, if morphological change is driven indirectly through food supply rather than directly through thermoregulation [@schmidt_concomitant_2005; @teplitsky_bergmanns_2008], species that depend most heavily on invertebrates should be the most sensitive, and dietary specialization should help explain variation among species in their trajectories.

Answering these questions at the scale of a biome requires a compiled trait database [@rodrigues_atlantic_2019], and compilations bring their own inferential hazard: because they aggregate records from many independent research programs, localities, protocols and seasons, apparent temporal trends can arise from changes in how the dataset was assembled rather than from phenotypic change [@weeks2020]. We therefore model sampling structure explicitly throughout, and compare estimates across a sequence of control tiers; the details are given in the Methods and the full model sequence in the Supplementary Material.

Here, we use 24 years (1995–2018) of morphological data from 73 passerine species (`r .n(desc$n_rec)` live-capture records; ATLANTIC BIRD TRAITS; @fig-map) to ask whether Atlantic Forest passerines show consistent morphological change across a period of regional warming. We characterize that response in three focal traits—body mass, wing length, and bill width—and then ask how it is structured: whether mass and wing length change in concert on the same individuals or depart from geometric isometry, whether morphology covaries with interannual temperature anomalies, whether among-individual phenotypic variability has changed, and whether dietary reliance on invertebrates explains variation among species.

# Results

## Regional warming across the sampling domain

The analytical dataset comprised `r desc$n_spp` passerine species and `r .n(desc$n_rec)` adult live-capture records (`r .n(desc$n_rec_wing)` wing records across 72 species), gathered between 1995 and 2018 across 357 localities spanning the latitudinal and elevational range of the Brazilian Atlantic Forest, from sea level to over 1,500 m (@fig-map). Filtering criteria are given in the Methods.

![Geographic distribution and multi-decadal sampling of `r desc$n_spp` passerine bird species across the Brazilian Atlantic Forest domain. Sampling localities are displayed separately for the early (1995–2006; $n = 2,370$ wing records, 93 coordinate sites, 12 contributors) and late (2013–2018; $n = 2,870$ wing records, 146 coordinate sites, 33 contributors) sampling periods across the biome. Points represent sampling localities coloured by mean wing length, illustrating the broad latitudinal and elevational range covered by the dataset.](images/fig-map.png){#fig-map}

Historical climate data extracted at the 357 capture localities (CRU-TS 4.09 / WorldClim 2.1) documented significant regional warming over the study period: mean annual temperature rose by +0.246°C/decade (95% CI: +0.076 to +0.415°C/decade), representing an average warming of +0.57°C across capture sites between 1995 and 2018. In contrast, precipitation (−44.7 mm/decade, 95% CI: −123.1 to +33.7 mm) and drought indices (SPEI-12: −0.256, 95% CI: −0.617 to +0.105) exhibited no significant directional trends.

These records were contributed by 42 research programs working in 139 named municipalities, and both the set of active programs and the geographic focus of sampling shifted substantially over the 24 years (Supplementary Fig. S1, S2). All analyses below therefore incorporate mixed-effects controls for contributor identity, spatial coordinates, elevation, season, moult status, and individual bird identity; estimates across the full sequence of control tiers are reported in Supplementary Tables S2 and S3.

## Wing length declines weakly, with strong heterogeneity among species

Model-free comparisons of per-species mean trait values between the early (1995–2006) and late (2013–2018) sampling periods showed substantial variation across the community (@fig-trends): wing length decreased in 43 species and increased in 18 (@fig-trends A), body mass decreased in 36 and increased in 26 (@fig-trends B), and bill width decreased in 13 and increased in 31 (@fig-trends C).

![Species-level trajectories of wing length, body mass, and bill width between early and late sampling periods. Paired per-species means between the early (1995–2006) and late (2013–2018) periods for (A) wing length ($n = 61$ species), (B) body mass ($n = 62$ species), and (C) bill width ($n = 44$ species) across Atlantic Forest passerines. Lines connect period means for each species, colored by direction of shift (red = decrease, blue = increase), illustrating the raw interspecific variation across the community.](images/fig-trends.png){#fig-trends}

Unadjusted models suggested a relatively steep decline in wing length over time ($\beta = `r cw_m0$b`$ mm per SD-year, 95% CI: `r cw_m0$lo` to `r cw_m0$hi`; `r cw_m0$dec` mm/decade, `r .s1(wing_pct_dec)`%/decade), but the estimated trend weakened substantially after accounting for contributor identity and the other sources of sampling turnover. In the fully adjusted model (M3), the community-level trajectory was modest and its uncertainty overlapped zero: $\beta = `r cw_m3$b`$ mm per SD-year (95% CI: `r cw_m3$lo` to `r cw_m3$hi`; `r cw_m3$dec` mm/decade, −1.04%/decade; @fig-wingtrend). Analyses restricted to complete cases ($n = 8,282$; $\beta = `r cw_m3_cc$b`$, 95% CI: `r cw_m3_cc$lo` to `r cw_m3_cc$hi`) and to within-contributor temporal change ($\beta = `r cw_m5src_within$b`$, 95% CI: `r cw_m5src_within$lo` to `r cw_m5src_within$hi`; `r cw_m5src_within$dec` mm/decade) produced similarly weak estimates, indicating that much of the apparent decline in the raw data was associated with changes in sampling structure rather than with a strong community-wide temporal shift. Estimates for every control tier, and for the unknown-sex (M6), first-capture (M7) and outlier-excluded (M3_noanom) sensitivity analyses, are given in Supplementary Table S2; all fall within the same modest range.

![Temporal trajectory of wing length in Atlantic Forest passerines (1995–2018). (A) Within-species-centred wing length over time across 8,478 records from 73 species, with annual means (points, sized by record count). The steep dashed line represents the unadjusted baseline model (M0: −1.84 mm/decade); the solid line represents the fully controlled phylogenetic model across 50 trees (M3: −0.74 mm/decade, 95% CI spanning zero). Inset displays wing records per year. (B) Zoomed view of annual means ($\pm 1.96$ SE) and fitted trajectories on the scale of the effect. Estimates and intervals are Rubin-pooled across 50 phylogenetic trees (`glmmTMB` `propto`).](images/fig-wingtrend.png){#fig-wingtrend}

Contributors with the longest continuous sampling spans likewise showed no directional wing change (E. Carrano: −0.01 mm/decade [−0.25, +0.24], $n = 1,040$; A. Ross: −0.29 [−1.28, +0.69], $n = 618$; M. Alves: −0.07 [−0.47, +0.32], $n = 433$), whereas the between-contributor term reflected substantial variation among programs ($\beta = `r cw_m5src_mean$b`$, 95% CI: `r cw_m5src_mean$lo` to `r cw_m5src_mean$hi`).

Species-specific slopes from the fully adjusted model showed pronounced interspecific heterogeneity (@fig-species-slopes): 49 of 72 species with wing measurements had negative point estimates, but 61 of 72 had 95% intervals overlapping zero. Only 9 species declined with intervals excluding zero, and 2 increased. The median species slope was −0.54 mm/decade. Overall, wing-length trajectories were weakly negative at the community level but highly heterogeneous among species, with substantial uncertainty around the average trend.

Forest plot of species-specific slopes (mm/decade) across 72 passerine species, ordered by rate of change. Horizontal bars show 95% intervals; filled circles denote species whose intervals exclude zero (red = negative, blue = positive), while open circles denote species whose intervals span zero ($n = 61$ species). Shaded vertical band and solid blue line indicate the pooled M3 year slope (−0.74 mm/decade, 95% CI: −1.55 to +0.07). Hollow grey circles indicate unadjusted baseline (M0) slopes.](images/fig-species-slopes.png){#fig-species-slopes}


## Little evidence of directional change in body mass

In contrast to the widespread body mass declines documented in the central Amazon [@jirinec2021morphological], we found little evidence of directional change in body mass across the 24-year record ($n = 11,077$ records). The unadjusted estimate was already slight and non-significant ($\beta = `r mass_m0$b`$ per SD-year, 95% CI: `r mass_m0$lo` to `r mass_m0$hi`; `r mass_m0$pct`%/decade), and it remained indistinguishable from zero under full adjustment ($\beta = `r mass_m3$b`$, 95% CI: `r mass_m3$lo` to `r mass_m3$hi`; `r mass_m3$pct`%/decade) and within contributors ($\beta = `r mass_within$b`$, 95% CI: `r mass_within$lo` to `r mass_within$hi`; `r mass_within$pct`%/decade). Unlike wing length, the body-mass estimate therefore changed little across control tiers (Supplementary Table S3).

Live-captured birds gained mass over the course of the day (+`r mass_hr_pct`% body mass per hour, 95% CI: `r mass_hr_lo` to `r mass_hr_hi`%, $t = 7.03$, $n = 8,345$), consistent with a normal diurnal feeding rhythm. Controlling for capture hour left the decadal slope flat ($\beta = `r mass_hour$b`$, 95% CI: `r mass_hour$lo` to `r mass_hour$hi`; `r mass_hour$pct`%/decade).

## Wing and mass are decoupled: a departure from geometric isometry

The more informative question is how the two traits changed together. We analyzed 7,577 shared capture events in which wing length and body mass were measured on the same individual, across 72 species. Because wing length is a linear dimension ($L^1$) whereas body mass reflects volume ($M \propto L^3$), an animal shrinking uniformly without changing shape—strict geometric isometry—would lose mass at approximately three times the rate of its linear shrinkage ($\% \Delta M \approx 3 \times \% \Delta L$).

On these shared records, wing length declined by `r iso_m1a_wing`%/decade (95% CI: `r iso_m1a_wing_lo` to `r iso_m1a_wing_hi`%) while body mass was stable (`r iso_m1a_mass`%/decade, 95% CI: `r iso_m1a_mass_lo` to `r iso_m1a_mass_hi`%; @fig-isometry A). Strict isometry would predict a mass decline of `r iso_m1a_exp`%/decade. The linear contrast ($\text{mass trend} - 3 \times \text{wing trend}$) was +`r iso_m1a_cont`%/decade (95% CI: `r iso_m1a_cont_lo` to `r iso_m1a_cont_hi`%, $z = 2.35$, $p = 0.019$; @fig-isometry A), excluding zero. The shared-individual data therefore reject strict geometric isometry: mass and wing length changed independently of one another, with mass retained relative to the small wing-length decline.

This departure does not depend on the parsimonious specification: refitting the contrast directly as a response under the full M3 adjustment set across 50 trees gives `r rr_iso_m3$pct`%/decade (95% CI: `r rr_iso_m3$lo` to `r rr_iso_m3$hi`%, $z = `r rr_iso_m3$z`$, $p `r rr_iso_m3$p`$), slightly larger than the parsimonious estimate. Fitting the contrast directly also yields its standard error exactly, without combining two separately estimated slopes.

In bivariate morphospace (@fig-isometry B), the Atlantic Forest community 95% confidence ellipse sits in the region of stasis and mild mass retention, and excludes the decoupling quadrant reported for the central Amazon [@jirinec2021morphological], where wings lengthened as body mass declined. We note that this contrast rejects proportional co-variation between mass and wing length; because wing length is itself a functionally labile trait that can change independently of overall structural size, it does not on its own establish a change in whole-body shape.

![Bivariate temporal allometry and test of geometric isometry on shared individuals. **(A)** Decadal rates of morphological change (% per decade) across 50 phylogenetic trees on 7,577 shared records (72 species) with simultaneous wing length and body mass measurements. Points and horizontal bars indicate estimates and 95% confidence intervals for observed wing length, observed body mass, expected isometric mass change under cubic geometric scaling ($M \propto L^3$), and the formal isometry contrast ($\Delta_{\text{iso}} = \Delta M - 3\Delta L$) under parsimonious contributor control (M1a; green diamond; $z = 2.35, p = 0.019$, rejecting isometry toward mass conservation/stoutening). The central Amazonian benchmark from @jirinec2021morphological is shown for comparison. **(B)** Bivariate morphological state space ($\Delta\text{Wing}$ vs. $\Delta\text{Mass}$). The solid black line indicates strict geometric isometry ($y = 3x$), the dotted line indicates equal rates ($y = x$), and shaded zones denote proportional shrinkage (blue) and morphological decoupling/slenderization (red). The green ellipse denotes the 95% confidence ellipse for the Atlantic Forest community under contributor control, encompassing mass stasis and excluding Amazonian slenderization. Semi-transparent circles represent species-specific controlled estimates ($n = 72$).](images/fig-isometry.png){#fig-isometry}

## Annual temperature anomalies do not explain the allometric shift

If the wing–mass shift tracks thermal conditions, individuals sampled in warmer-than-usual years should depart further from isometry. We tested this by linking each capture to the local annual temperature anomaly ($\Delta T_{\text{local}}$: the capture-year mean temperature at the record's coordinates, minus that locality's own long-run mean; WorldClim historical monthly weather, CRU-TS 4.09 downscaled).

We found no support for it. Under the same M3 adjustment set used for the temporal models, the isometry contrast was not associated with the annual anomaly ($\beta = `r rr_iso_therm$b`$, 95% CI: `r rr_iso_therm$lo` to `r rr_iso_therm$hi`, $z = `r rr_iso_therm$z`$, $p `r rr_iso_therm$p`$; `r rr_iso_therm$trees` of 50 trees converged), and neither were wing length ($z = `r rr_wing_therm$z`$, $p `r rr_wing_therm$p`$) or body mass ($z = `r rr_mass_therm$z`$, $p `r rr_mass_therm$p`$). The null result is not an artefact of one specification. The anomaly effect on the isometry contrast remains indistinguishable from zero when calendar year and the anomaly are entered simultaneously ($z = `r rr_iso_therm_e1$z`$), when the anomaly is detrended within sites ($z = `r rr_iso_therm_e1b$z`$), and when a locality-year random intercept is added to reflect the fact that all birds caught at one site in one year share a single anomaly value ($z = `r rr_iso_therm_e2$z`$). All four specifications are tabulated in Supplementary Note S8.

What does track the contrast is calendar time. In a model containing both, the year term is clearly non-zero ($z = `r rr_iso_yr$z`$, $p `r rr_iso_yr$p`$) while the anomaly is not ($z = `r rr_iso_therm_e1$z`$). We therefore report the allometric shift as a temporal change and make no claim that interannual thermal variation drives it. We note in addition that capture-year temperature is a poor candidate exposure for a fixed adult wing length, which is grown once at moult; any thermal mechanism would have to act during development rather than in the year of capture.

## Bill width shows little temporal change

Allen's rule [@allen1877; @ryding2021shape] posits that extremities such as bills enlarge in warm climates to facilitate non-evaporative thermoregulatory heat dissipation. Raw species-level trajectories for bill width displayed both increases and decreases across the community (@fig-trends C). In an unadjusted baseline model without contributor controls (M0), bill width appeared to show a statistically significant positive decadal trend: $\beta = +`r bill_m0$b2`$ mm per SD-year (95% CI: +`r bill_m0$lo2` to +`r bill_m0$hi2`, $t = 2.6$, $n = `r bill_m0$n`$), a pattern that at face value would be consistent with Allen-type expectations.

However, when contributor identity was accounted for (M1), this apparent positive trajectory reversed direction ($\beta = `r bill_m1a$b2`$ mm/SD-year, 95% CI: `r bill_m1a$lo2` to `r bill_m1a$hi2`, $n = `r bill_m1a$n`$). In the fully controlled 50-tree phylogenetic model (M3), bill width remained flat: $\beta = `r bill_m3$b2`$ mm/SD-year (95% CI: `r bill_m3$lo2` to `r bill_m3$hi2`, corresponding to −0.03 mm/decade, $n = `r bill_m3$n`$). Evaluating temporal change within the same contributor gave a similarly flat estimate ($\beta = +`r bill_within$b2`$ mm/SD-year, 95% CI: `r bill_within$lo2` to `r bill_within$hi2`). The apparent baseline increase was therefore not robust to the inclusion of contributor identity; because contributors differ in sampling geography as well as in measurement practice, we cannot separate these explanations. Taken together, these analyses give little evidence of bill-width change of the kind expected under Allen-type thermoregulatory predictions. We note that this is a test of temporal change within populations during a warming period, not a test of the ecogeographical pattern that Allen's rule describes.

## Little evidence of change in among-individual phenotypic variability

Climate warming has been hypothesized to alter phenotypic variance as well as trait means [@teplitsky_climate_2014]. Apparent increases in among-individual variability were, however, sensitive to sampling structure.

Our primary analysis used continuous heteroscedastic dispersion models, which estimate temporal change in residual standard deviation ($\sigma$) from the full continuous time series while adjusting for covariates [`glmmTMB` `dispformula`; @williams2025glmmtmb]. Unadjusted, $\sigma$ appeared to increase by +9.6%/decade (95% CI: +6.3 to +13.0%). Adding contributor random intercepts to the dispersion model reversed the estimate to −6.3%/decade (95% CI: −13.4 to +1.5%), overlapping zero. Adding time-resolved local temperature to the dispersion model yielded no association between residual variance and thermal conditions (−0.7% per SD temperature, 95% CI: −8.7 to +8.1%, $z = −0.16$).

Species-level $\ln\text{CVR}$ comparisons between early (1995–2006) and late (2013–2018) periods gave the same picture. Pooled across contributors, variability appeared to increase (wing length $\ln\text{CVR} = +0.177$, 95% CI: 0.031 to 0.323, $k = 54$; body mass $+0.193$, 95% CI: 0.021 to 0.366, $k = 57$; bill width $+0.068$, 95% CI: −0.146 to +0.282, $k = 36$; Supplementary Fig. S10). But later samples also drew on more contributors per species-period cell (3.68 early versus 5.50 late, Wilcoxon $p = 5 \times 10^{-8}$), whose residual standard deviations differed up to 2.5-fold. Restricted to within the same contributor, the apparent expansion disappeared ($\ln\text{CVR} = −0.249$, 95% CI: −0.515 to +0.017; $k = 15$).

Evidence for increasing phenotypic variability therefore largely disappears once contributor turnover is accounted for, and residual variance was not clearly associated with annual temperature. Because contributors also differ in localities, protocols, and the field workers they employ, this comparison removes pooling across contributors rather than isolating biological variance from observational heterogeneity more generally.

## Dietary specialization and morphological change

To test whether dietary reliance on invertebrates buffered or accelerated morphological trajectories, we examined species' diet composition from EltonTraits. In continuous interaction models (Model A; @fig-dietinteraction, top panel), baseline models suggested a positive interaction between year and invertebrate diet proportion ($\beta = +0.663$, 95% CI: +0.217 to +1.108; $z = 2.92$). However, adding contributor intercepts halved this interaction to $\beta = +0.319$ (95% CI: −0.019 to +0.657; $z = 1.85$), with the confidence interval spanning zero. Categorical comparisons (Model B: Invertebrate vs Other; @fig-dietinteraction, bottom panel) similarly attenuated under controls ($\beta = +0.387$, 95% CI: −0.335 to +1.109).

Across all models, the decadal slope for obligate insectivores (species at the 90th percentile of invertebrate diet) was indistinguishable from zero (−0.15 mm/decade, 95% CI: −0.67 to +0.52). Dietary reliance on invertebrates therefore did not clearly explain variation in wing-length trajectories: apparent interactions in simpler models weakened substantially after accounting for contributor identity, and estimated temporal slopes for highly insectivorous species overlapped zero. We found little evidence that trophic specialization systematically modified morphological responses over the study period, but the interaction is estimated with considerable uncertainty and we cannot exclude an effect of moderate size.

![Decadal wing-length change as a function of dietary reliance on invertebrates. (Top) Predicted change in wing length (mm) over time across the 10th (p10, blue), 50th (p50, orange), and 90th (p90, red) species-weighted percentiles of invertebrate diet proportion (continuous Model A), with shaded ribbons denoting Rubin-pooled 95% uncertainty across 50 phylogenetic trees. (Bottom) Predicted wing trajectories for species categorized by primary diet (Model B: Invertebrate vs Other diet). Under full controls (+ contributor), the interaction attenuates and obligate insectivores exhibit slopes overlapping zero.](images/diet_interaction_plot.png){#fig-dietinteraction}

Whether regional invertebrate availability changed over the same period could not be assessed directly: no standardized, multi-decadal prey monitoring exists for Atlantic Forest understorey. An exploratory analysis of litter-ant richness, an imperfect and indirect proxy, is reported in Supplementary Note S7.

## Robustness: century-scale context and sampling breadth

Two checks bear on how far the 1995–2018 results generalize: whether the contemporary patterns fall within the range of historical background variation, and how sensitive they are to our filtering decisions. Both are context rather than primary analyses, and both carry limitations we set out here. Full results are in Supplementary Notes S3 and S4.

Two-phase piecewise linear regression on secular regional temperature anomalies (NASA GISS Zonal $24^\circ\text{S}\text{–Equator}$, 1880–2018; @lenssen2019gistemp) was fitted with the breakpoint fixed a priori at 1980, the conventional onset of the modern warming era rather than a value estimated from these data (Supplementary Fig. S4; see Methods). Before 1980 regional temperatures changed little ($+0.036^\circ\text{C}$/decade, 95% CI: $+0.002$ to $+0.070$, $t = 2.05, p = 0.042$); after 1980 warming was more than five-fold faster ($+0.190^\circ\text{C}$/decade, 95% CI: $+0.147$ to $+0.233$, $t = 8.62, p < 10^{-15}$), matching the rate across our modern capture sites (+0.25°C/decade).

Historical museum study skins ($n = 3,439$ adult specimens across 142 passerine species, 1884–2017; MZUSP, MNRJ, FURB, UFPE) show no wing-length decline before 1980 ($+0.45$ mm/decade, $t = 3.71$; Supplementary Fig. S4), and body mass in historical specimens (1962–1979) shows no detectable trend ($-0.17\%$/year, $t = -0.65, p = 0.52$; Supplementary Fig. S5). The useful conclusion from the historical material is therefore a narrow one: the contemporary patterns are not the continuation of a long-running trajectory, because no such trajectory is visible in the historical record.

We do not, however, read the combined series as evidence of a morphological change emerging after 1980, because the estimate is not robust to how the two data sources are joined. Across the `r rr_sec_asrun$n` records of the 175 species that span both eras, the decline under the specification we ran is `r rr_sec_asrun$pct`%/decade (95% CI: `r rr_sec_asrun$lo` to `r rr_sec_asrun$hi`%, $t = `r rr_sec_asrun$t`$). But it is carried entirely by the live captures (`r rr_sec_live$pct`%/decade, $t = `r rr_sec_live$t`$, $n = `r rr_sec_live$n`$); museum specimens alone show no trend at all (`r rr_sec_museum$pct2`%/decade, $t = `r rr_sec_museum$t`$, $n = `r rr_sec_museum$n`$), and the year $\times$ source interaction is clearly non-zero ($t = `r rr_sec_intx$t`$). A source intercept, which is what the model includes, cannot absorb a difference in slopes.

Age composition compounds this. The combined series pools all age classes, whereas the primary analysis is restricted to adults, and the proportion of adults falls steadily across the record ($\beta = `r .s4(rr_age[2,1])`$ per year, $z = `r .s(rr_age[2,3])`$, $p < 10^{-15}$). Restricting the spanning cohort to adults leaves the decline indistinguishable from zero (`r rr_sec_adults$pct`%/decade, 95% CI: `r rr_sec_adults$lo` to `r rr_sec_adults$hi`%, $t = `r rr_sec_adults$t`$, $n = `r rr_sec_adults$n`$). We therefore report the historical material only as evidence of no prior trend, and draw no quantitative inference about century-scale rates.

Expanding the analytical scope to mirror the less restrictive sampling of @jirinec2021morphological—birds of unknown sex, all age classes, all understorey mist-netted orders ($n = 46,663$ captures across 243 species; Supplementary Fig. S7; Supplementary Table S1)—left wing-length trajectories consistent with our focal estimates ($-1.00\%$/decade, 95% CI: $-2.09$ to $+0.09\%$; $-0.76$ mm/decade). In that four-fold larger sample body mass declined by $-1.29\%$/decade (95% CI: $-2.30$ to $-0.27\%$, $t = -2.47, p = 0.014$; Supplementary Table S1), a trend not detectable in the restricted sample. We report the absence of a body-mass trend as a conclusion specific to the filtered sample rather than a general one.

# Discussion

Do the pronounced morphological responses reported for central Amazonian birds generalize to tropical forest birds more broadly? Across 73 passerine species and 24 years of regional warming in the Brazilian Atlantic Forest, our answer is that they largely do not. Morphological change in this community was weak, heterogeneous among species, and in several cases not separable from changes in how the dataset was assembled. Ordered as in the Results, we find:
(1) **Weak and heterogeneous wing-length change**: The community-level trajectory was modestly negative with a confidence interval overlapping zero (−0.74 mm/decade; within-contributor slope −0.32 mm/decade), and 61 of 72 species had intervals overlapping zero.
(2) **No detectable change in body mass**: Unlike in the central Amazon, we found little evidence of directional change (−0.91%/decade, spanning zero), and unlike wing length this estimate was stable across control tiers.
(3) **Mass–wing decoupling**: On shared individuals, body mass was more conserved than cubic geometric shrinkage of the wing predicts (+4.85%/decade contrast, $p = 0.019$), rejecting strict geometric isometry.
(4) **No thermal signal behind the allometric shift**: The departure from isometry was not associated with annual temperature anomalies under the full adjustment set ($z = `r rr_iso_therm$z`$, $p `r rr_iso_therm$p`$); calendar time, not interannual thermal variation, tracks the change.
(5) **Little evidence of bill-width change**: Bill width showed no detectable temporal expansion (−0.03 mm/decade), giving little evidence of the extremity enlargement expected under Allen-type thermoregulatory predictions.
(6) **Little evidence of change in phenotypic variability**: Apparent increases in among-individual variability did not survive adjustment for contributor turnover, and residual variance did not track temperature.
(7) **No clear dietary modulation**: Temporal slopes for highly insectivorous species overlapped zero, giving little evidence that trophic specialization amplified morphological sensitivity, though the interaction remains uncertain.

## Interspecific variation and departure from geometric isometry

Rather than a uniform community-wide response, our results reveal substantial interspecific heterogeneity (@fig-species-slopes). While a small minority of species exhibited declines in wing length whose confidence intervals excluded zero (9 of 72 species) or comparable increases (2 of 72 species), the vast majority (61 species) showed trajectories overlapping zero. This diversity of species trajectories aligns with recent global syntheses showing that morphological responses to climate change are frequently idiosyncratic and species-specific rather than uniform [@teplitsky_climate_2014].

Importantly, our analysis of 7,577 shared records from the same individuals revealed that body mass was more conserved than predicted under cubic geometric scaling of wing shortening. Mass and wing length are therefore decoupled, and the data reject strict geometric isometry; rather than the slenderization documented in the Amazon [@jirinec2021morphological], Atlantic Forest passerines retain mass relative to wing length. Dietary reliance on invertebrates did not clearly explain variation in these trajectories: obligate insectivores exhibited a temporal slope overlapping zero, giving little evidence that trophic specialization modified morphological responses over this period, though the interaction remains uncertain.

## Contrasting macroecological dynamics: the Atlantic Forest and the central Amazon

These findings present a macroecological contrast to the only comparable multi-decadal Neotropical benchmark: the study by @jirinec2021morphological in the central Amazon. In 77 non-migratory understorey species monitored over 40 years in continuous primary rainforest, @jirinec2021morphological documented widespread declines in body mass (averaging −0.1 to −0.2%/year) coupled with wing elongation in 36% of species. This resulted in a community-wide reduction in wing loading, interpreted as an adaptation to lower metabolic flight costs and improve flight efficiency in an increasingly hot, dry understorey.

The two datasets therefore give different pictures. Before considering why, we note that this is a contrast between two studies rather than a controlled comparison: the Atlantic Forest analysis and the Amazonian study differ not only in landscape context but also in sampling design, temporal coverage, species composition, and measurement structure, and part of the difference may reside in these features. With that caveat, three non-mutually exclusive ecological and evolutionary hypotheses could contribute to a genuine difference. Our data do not discriminate among them, and we present them as hypotheses for future work rather than as conclusions:

First, **landscape fragmentation and aerodynamic flight constraints**. The central Amazonian study was conducted in a continuous, undisturbed primary forest block (BDFFP) where birds move beneath a continuous closed canopy. In continuous understorey, foraging flights are typically short, highly maneuverable sallies; under such conditions, longer wings and lower wing loading reduce metabolic transport costs with minimal aerodynamic penalty [@jirinec2021morphological]. In contrast, the Atlantic Forest has undergone extensive historical deforestation, leaving a heavily fragmented landscape where forest patches are embedded in open agricultural or pastoral matrices [@ribeiro2009atlantic]. In fragmented landscapes, forest birds must frequently traverse open matrix, cross habitat edges, and navigate areas exposed to strong winds and elevated predation from open-country raptors [@ribeiro2009atlantic]. Under these conditions, aerodynamic performance demands flight power, burst speed, and high maneuverability rather than low wing loading. Selective pressures to navigate fragmented landscapes may therefore penalize wing lengthening or body mass reduction, constraining morphological shifts that might otherwise be favored in continuous forest.

Second, **topographic complexity and elevational thermal refugia**. The central Amazon BDFFP site occupies a relatively flat lowland landscape (elevation ~50–150 m) where species have limited access to steep thermal gradients and cannot escape regional warming through short-distance elevational shifts. In contrast, the Atlantic Forest features steep coastal mountain systems (e.g., Serra do Mar, Serra da Mantiqueira) spanning elevations from sea level to over 2,000 m. This complex topography generates sharp microclimatic gradients across short horizontal distances. Birds in topographically complex biomes may buffer themselves against rising temperatures by making subtle elevational or microhabitat shifts, reducing the physiological pressure to undergo morphological adaptation.

Third, **microclimatic variability and physiological plasticity**. Forest fragments experience pronounced edge effects, with higher temperature variability and fluctuating humidity relative to continuous interior forest. Atlantic Forest birds may already possess high physiological tolerance and plastic buffering capacity to cope with variable microclimates, which would reduce the necessity for directional morphological change over multi-decadal timescales. We emphasise that we did not test this: the diurnal body mass gains recorded here (+0.40%/hour) reflect the normal within-day feeding rhythm and are not evidence of thermal plasticity.

Beyond these ecological mechanisms, a plausible alternative hypothesis is whether the contrast reflects study design—namely, a single continuous 40-year ringing station (BDFFP) versus a multi-site macroecological compilation. Our within-contributor Mundlak decomposition makes this less likely as a complete explanation: contributors who sampled birds continuously across multi-year spans (e.g., E. Carrano, A. Ross, M. Alves) independently exhibited slopes indistinguishable from zero (within-contributor wing slope: `r cw_m5src_within$dec` mm/decade; complete cases: +0.03 mm/decade; body mass: `r mass_within$pct`%/decade). Restricting the temporal comparison to within a single contributor removes confounding from turnover among research programs, but it does not remove change over time in the individual field workers, localities, or protocols operating within a program, so it constrains rather than eliminates a sampling explanation.

## Evaluating ecogeographical rules in tropical endotherms

Our findings provide a critical empirical test of classic ecogeographical rules in tropical endotherms under climate change. Bergmann's rule has frequently been generalized as a general expectation that warming temperatures drive reductions in animal body size [@gardner_declining_2011; @sheridan_shrinking_2011]. In our 24-year dataset of 73 tropical passerine species, we found little evidence of directional change in body mass despite +0.25°C/decade of regional warming. This challenges the generality of Bergmann's rule in tropical forest birds, and indicates that tropical endotherms need not show detectable body-mass loss over decadal timescales.

Similarly, Allen's rule posits that appendages enlarge in warmer environments to facilitate heat dissipation [@allen1877; @ryding2021shape]. While unadjusted baseline models suggested a temporal increase in bill width, this apparent trend did not survive the inclusion of contributor identity, leaving little evidence of bill-width change. In tropical passerines, bill morphology is heavily constrained by foraging biomechanics, trophic specialization, and vocal performance, which may strongly override subtle thermoregulatory selection for larger bills [@teplitsky_climate_2014].

## The inferential foundation for macroecological trait synthesis

Our study highlights the role of proper data dependency controls when analyzing multi-decadal compilations in macroecology. Large-scale compilations such as ATLANTIC BIRD TRAITS [@rodrigues_atlantic_2019] are indispensable for macroecological and macroevolutionary research, providing taxonomic and geographic scope that single-site studies cannot achieve. However, because compiled databases combine measurements across dozens of independent research teams, sampling localities, protocols, and seasons, apparent multi-decadal trends can be substantially confounded by sampling turnover.

In our dataset, unadjusted baseline models suggested steep declines in wing length, increases in bill width, and expanding trait variability. Under our multi-tiered comparative framework, the estimated wing decline attenuated by approximately 60%, the apparent bill expansion disappeared, and the apparent variance inflation was no longer supported. Because contributor identity, sampling geography, protocol, and season are not fully separable in a compilation of this kind, we do not attribute this attenuation to any single source; what the comparison establishes is that the unadjusted estimates were substantially carried by how the dataset was assembled. Adding contributor identity and individual identity as random intercepts, and latitude, longitude, elevation, season, and moult as fixed effects—alongside 50-tree phylogenetic comparative models—provided the inferential foundation necessary to uncover these biological patterns. Rather than invalidating trait compilations, our findings indicate that large-scale compilations can yield robust macroecological insight when sampling structure is modelled explicitly.

## Secular context and sampling breadth

Our focal analytical dataset spanned 24 years (1995–2018), corresponding to the era of standardized, multi-project mist-netting in the Atlantic Forest. Century-scale instrumental climate data and historical museum collections bear on two questions: did morphological stability precede this window, and how sensitive are our inferences to taxonomic and demographic sampling breadth?

First, the historical material shows no morphological trend before 1980, across decades in which regional temperatures changed little. The contemporary patterns are therefore not the tail of a long-running trajectory. We stop there. The stronger claim—that morphological change emerged with the post-1980 acceleration of warming—would require the combined museum-plus-live series, and that series does not support it: the apparent secular decline is carried entirely by the live captures, disappears in museum specimens alone, and does not survive restriction to adults (Results, §Robustness). Because museum preparation shrinks feathers and keratin, and because we have no sample measured by both routes with which to calibrate the offset, joining the two sources introduces exactly the kind of artefact our primary analysis excludes skins to avoid.

Second, expanding the analytical framework to mirror less restrictive community sampling shows that our conclusions are not uniformly robust to filtering decisions, and it is worth distinguishing which are. The wing-length result is robust: across the broader avian understorey community, and across all analytical strata and the century-long series, wing-length trajectories remained negative or neutral, and we found no sign of the wing elongation and reduced wing loading reported for the contiguous Amazon. The body-mass result is more sensitive: the community-wide analysis revealed a modest decline that is not detectable in the restricted 73-species sample. Whether this reflects greater statistical power, the inclusion of species or demographic classes excluded from the primary sample, or residual sampling structure in the broader compilation, we cannot determine here, and we therefore treat the absence of a body-mass trend as a conclusion specific to the filtered sample. The resulting position of the Atlantic Forest, between temperate migratory species and the undisturbed central Amazonian understorey, is suggestive but rests on a cross-study comparison and a single modest estimate; we do not regard it as establishing quantitatively intermediate thermal sensitivity.

In summary, 24 years of climate warming in the Brazilian Atlantic Forest have not induced the widespread body mass loss or wing elongation observed in the continuous Amazonian understorey. Instead, we found little evidence of directional change in body mass or bill width, a departure from geometric isometry in which mass is retained relative to wing length, and subtle, species-specific adjustments in wing length. These contrasting responses suggest that landscape fragmentation, topographic complexity, and ecological context shape how tropical species respond to anthropogenic climate change, a hypothesis that our cross-study comparison motivates but cannot itself test.

# Methods {#sec-methods}

## Trait database filtering and analytical sample derivation

We extracted avian morphological measurements from the ATLANTIC BIRD TRAITS database [@rodrigues_atlantic_2019], a comprehensive data compilation comprising `r .n(desc$raw_total)` morphometric entries across the Brazilian Atlantic Forest domain, of which passerines represent `r desc$raw_pass_pct`% (`r .n(desc$raw_passerine)` records). To ensure that temporal analyses reflect genuine living phenotypic variation rather than methodological or preservation artifacts, we implemented a rigorous multi-stage filtering protocol.

First, we restricted the dataset strictly to live field captures, excluding museum study skins. Museum preparation induces marked, non-linear post-mortem shrinkage in feathers, bill keratin, and skeletal dimensions (typically 1–3% reduction in linear dimensions upon drying; @weeks2020). Because museum specimens in regional collections are heavily concentrated in earlier decades of the 20th century, retaining study skins introduces artificial positive temporal trends. Second, we restricted records to adult individuals (`Age == "Adult"`), excluding juveniles and fledglings whose flight feathers and bills are incompletely developed. Third, we filtered records spatially to sampling localities falling within a 20-km buffer of the Brazilian Atlantic Forest biome boundary (IBGE/MMA official shapefile), eliminating captures situated in adjacent Cerrado or Caatinga enclaves. The 20-km allowance is the tolerance already applied in the ATLANTIC BIRD TRAITS compilation itself, and it accommodates coordinate imprecision and the fact that the mapped biome boundary is a generalization of a gradual ecotone; it is not a biological buffer and no result depends on its exact width. Fourth, we bounded the temporal window to 1995–2018 (24 calendar years), representing the era of active multi-project mist-netting in the biome with consistent capture documentation. We did not filter on migratory status: the compilation does not record it, and we therefore make no claim that the focal species are strictly resident. The sample comprises the passerines captured by Atlantic Forest mist-netting programs, which may include partial or altitudinal migrants.

Finally, to guarantee robust parameter estimation for species-level random intercepts and random slopes, we restricted the primary analytical sample to species with $\ge 30$ live-capture records and a temporal sampling span of $\ge 5$ years. This yielded an analytical dataset of `r desc$n_spp` passerine species and `r .n(desc$n_rec)` live-capture records (`r .n(desc$n_rec_wing)` wing-length records across 72 species; one species, *Herpsilochmus pectoralis*, was sampled exclusively for bill and tarsus traits and lacked wing and mass records in the compilation). Wing length was coalesced across database columns, prioritizing right wing length when specified, followed by left wing length and unspecified wing length (`conc.wing.length`). A parallel dataset including unsexed adult individuals ($n = 3,532$) was compiled to evaluate whether patterns replicated in birds lacking sex determination.

## Accounting for contributor turnover and spatial provenance

In large-scale macroecological compilations aggregating data across independent research programs, two structural factors can confound temporal trends if left unmodeled: contributor turnover and spatial turnover.

### Contributor turnover and research-group random effects

In avian morphometrics, inter-observer measurement error is well-documented to reach 1–3 mm for wing length and 0.5–1 mm for bill dimensions [@weeks2020]. If different field workers apply slightly different caliper tension or wing-flattening techniques, and if the set of active research programs changes over time, apparent temporal trends in morphology can arise entirely through turnover in who contributed the data.

In the ATLANTIC BIRD TRAITS compilation, the field measurer column (`Measurer`) is 100% missing (NA), so the individual who took each measurement cannot be identified. The identity of the principal investigator and research group coordinator (`Main_researcher`) is, however, 100% complete across all analytical records, comprising 42 distinct entries in our wing dataset. **Throughout this paper we refer to this grouping variable as the *contributor*, meaning the research group or project that supplied the record, and we use this single term consistently in place of "observer" or "measurer".** We emphasise that the contributor is a proxy rather than a direct measure of measurement practice: a contributor random effect absorbs whatever is shared among records originating from the same research program, which includes caliper and wing-flattening conventions, but also field protocols, target habitats, the set of localities worked, and project-specific species composition. Attenuation of a temporal trend after adding this term therefore indicates that the trend was partly carried by differences among research programs, and does not by itself isolate measurement error from these other, partly inseparable, sources.

An audit revealed high contributor turnover across the 24-year record: only 6 of the 42 contributors sampled birds in both the early (1995–2006) and late (2013–2018) periods, while the late period experienced an influx of 33 active contributors compared to 12 early (Supplementary Fig. S1). To account for baseline differences among research programs, we incorporated a random intercept for contributor identity (`(1 | Main_researcher)`).

### Spatial provenance and continuous environmental controls

Over the 24-year timeframe, geographical sampling shifted substantially: early captures (1995–2006) were heavily concentrated in the southern Atlantic Forest (mean latitude $-24.8^\circ$), whereas later captures (2013–2018) expanded northwards (mean latitude $-21.9^\circ$) and into higher elevations (median altitude shifting from 175 m to 489 m). Because widespread passerines frequently exhibit ecogeographical clines in body size, geographic turnover across sampling periods can easily mimic temporal phenotypic change.

To account for continuous spatial and elevational variation without discarding records or introducing artificial clustering, models incorporated standardized latitude (`scaled_lat`), standardized longitude (`scaled_long`), and standardized elevation (`scaled_elev`) as continuous covariates.

### Sampling hierarchy, collinearity, and exclusion of administrative municipality

Another structural consideration in multi-source macroecological databases is the hierarchical relationship between research teams and geographic sampling units. Across the 24-year ATLANTIC BIRD TRAITS compilation, individual field projects were typically conducted by distinct research groups operating within specific municipal territories. Consequently, spatial and contributor grouping factors exhibit substantial collinearity: in our shared analytical sample ($n = 7,577$), 110 of 128 municipalities (85.9%) were sampled by only a single contributor (and across the full body mass dataset, 129 of 150 municipalities, 86.0%, were sampled by a single contributor). Administrative municipalities are therefore largely nested within contributors rather than orthogonally crossed.

Because measurement conventions (caliper tension, wing flattening, scale calibration) are a property of the research program rather than of administrative municipal boundaries, and because geographic and altitudinal clines are directly controlled via continuous coordinates and elevation, incorporating a redundant `(1 | Municipality)` random intercept induces variance competition, collinearity, and parameter inflation without improving model fit. We therefore adopted the parsimonious contributor model (`(1 | Main_researcher)`) across all univariate and bivariate model tiers, avoiding collinear crossed random effects while ensuring robust parameter estimation and biological interpretability.

## Model sequence and within-between decomposition

To rigorously evaluate how dataset structure influences temporal trends, we fitted a ladder of increasingly controlled mixed-effects models across sequential tiers:

- **M0 (Baseline)**: Replicating published unadjusted model structures, accounting only for sex, calendar year (`scaled_yr`, centered and divided by its standard deviation, SD = 5.02 years), latitude (`scaled_lat`), species-specific random slopes and intercepts `(1 + scaled_yr || Binomial)`, and phylogenetic covariance `propto(0 + species_name | g, A)`.
- **M1**: Adding a random intercept for contributor identity `(1 | Main_researcher)` to absorb systematic differences among research programs, including but not limited to measurement conventions.
- **M2**: Adding fixed effects for protocol proxy (`wing_col`: right wing, left wing, or side unspecified), standardized longitude (`scaled_long`), and standardized elevation (`scaled_elev`).
- **M3 (Fully controlled model)**: Adding fixed effects for seasonal quarter (DJF: Dec–Feb; MAM: Mar–May; JJA: Jun–Aug; SON: Sep–Nov) to account for feather wear across the annual cycle, active primary moult status (`Molt`), and individual bird band identity `(1 | ID_individual)` (Ring $\times$ Species) to account for repeated captures of banded individuals.
- **Within-between decomposition (Mundlak REWB)**: To separate temporal change occurring within a single contributor from compositional turnover across contributors, calendar year was partitioned into the contributor mean capture year ($\bar{Y}_j = \text{yr\_src\_mean}$) and individual capture deviations from that contributor mean ($Y_{ij} - \bar{Y}_j = \text{yr\_within\_src}$) [@mundlak1978pooling; @bell2019fixed]. The within-contributor coefficient $\beta_{\text{within}}$ measures whether birds contributed by the *same* research program changed over time, and is therefore not driven by turnover in which programs were active. It does not, however, remove change over time in the individual field workers, localities, or protocols operating within a program.
- **Robustness and sensitivity tiers**:
  - `M3_cc`: The full M3 specification on complete cases ($n = 8,282$). The primary M3 sample ($n = 8,478$) does not discard records with incomplete covariates; instead, missingness is encoded explicitly. Records lacking a recorded altitude take a value imputed from other records at the same coordinates, and season and moult carry an explicit `unrecorded` level rather than being dropped. `M3_cc` removes the 196 records with an imputed altitude or an unrecorded season, so the contrast between M3 and `M3_cc` isolates the effect of that encoding.
  - `M6`: The M3 specification evaluated in birds of unknown sex ($n = 3,532$), to verify that findings generalize beyond sexable individuals. The `Sex` term is necessarily dropped, since every record in this subset is of unknown sex; the model is otherwise identical to M3.
  - `M7`: The full M3 specification restricted strictly to first captures ($n = 7,791$) to exclude any potential bias from recapture histories.
  - `M3_noanom`: The full M3 model re-fitted after excluding six anomalous sampling blocks (193 records). Blocks are contributor $\times$ municipality $\times$ year cells. For each record we took the deviation of its wing length from its own species $\times$ sex mean, averaged those deviations within each cell, and flagged cells with at least 10 records whose mean deviation exceeded 6 mm in absolute value. The 6 mm threshold is roughly 1.5 residual standard deviations of the M3 fit and about 8% of a typical wing; a shift of that size shared across an entire contributor-site-year block is more consistent with a protocol or data-entry change than with phenotypic variation. Two contributors' late blocks sit 9–12 mm below species means and account for most of the within-contributor decline, which is why the screen exists.

## Phylogenetic comparative analysis across 50 topologies

Taxonomic reconciliation between the ATLANTIC BIRD TRAITS database and the complete, dynamic avian phylogeny of @mctavish2025tree was executed using the four-stage matching cascade of `prepR4pcm` [@nakagawa2026prepr4pcm]: exact binomial matching, punctuation/spacing normalization, taxonomic synonym resolution via BirdLife International and IOC checklists, and fuzzy string matching. All 73 passerine species were audited and successfully mapped to phylogenetic tip labels with zero unplaced taxa.

To accommodate phylogenetic uncertainty, we drew 50 alternative phylogenetic topologies from the posterior distribution of @mctavish2025tree. For each tree, we computed the phylogenetic correlation matrix $A$ under a Brownian motion model of trait evolution. Fitting full multi-level models across 50 trees by MCMC is computationally prohibitive for random-effect structures of this complexity. We therefore fitted all models by restricted maximum likelihood using the `propto` covariance structure in `glmmTMB` v1.1.14 [@williams2025glmmtmb], which admits an arbitrary fixed correlation matrix scaled by an estimated variance:
```r
glmmTMB(formula = conc.wing.length ~ Sex + scaled_yr + scaled_lat + scaled_long + 
          scaled_elev + season + Molt + (1 + scaled_yr || Binomial) + 
          (1 | Main_researcher) + (1 | ID_individual) + 
          propto(0 + species_name | g, A),
        data = dat, REML = TRUE)
```
where `g` is a dummy grouping factor assigning all observations to a single covariance structure governed by matrix `A`. The phylogenetic covariance applies to the species intercepts only. Species-specific year slopes are estimated in the separate, non-phylogenetic term `(1 + scaled_yr || Binomial)`, so slopes are modelled as independent among species rather than as a Brownian process.

Parameter estimates $\hat{\beta}_k$ and variance-covariance matrices $V_k$ across the 50 converged trees were pooled using Rubin's rules [@nakagawa2019rubin; @nakagawa2026prepr4pcm]:
$$\bar{\beta} = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^K \hat{\beta}_k, \quad V_{\text{total}} = \bar{V} + \left(1 + \frac{1}{K}\right) B$$
where $\bar{V} = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^K V_k$ is the mean within-tree variance and $B = \frac{1}{K-1}\sum_{k=1}^K (\hat{\beta}_k - \bar{\beta})(\hat{\beta}_k - \bar{\beta})^\top$ is the between-tree variance. Wald-Rubin 95% confidence intervals were computed as $\bar{\beta} \pm 1.96 \sqrt{\operatorname{diag}(V_{\text{total}})}$.

## Body mass and bill width modeling and testing Allen's rule

To evaluate whether temporal shifts occurred in body mass and extremity dimensions, we applied the sequential control ladder to log-transformed body mass ($n = 11,077$) and bill width ($n = 3,205$). Bill width is the appendage measure used here because it is the extremity trait with the broadest coverage in the compilation and because bill surface is the principal avian site of non-evaporative heat exchange, which is the dimension Allen-type predictions concern. It is, however, a single and imperfect proxy: tarsus length is recorded for fewer individuals, and we did not analyse bill depth or surface area, so our test addresses one extremity dimension rather than heat-dissipating surface as a whole. Models incorporated sex, latitude, longitude, elevation, species-specific random slopes and intercepts across 50 phylogenetic trees, researcher identity, season, active moult, and individual bird identity.

To evaluate diurnal feeding rhythms in body mass, we extracted recorded capture time (`Hour`) for the 8,345 mass records with available time stamps. Diurnal mass gain was estimated from a model that is not the full M3 specification: `ln_body_mass ~ Sex + scaled_yr + scaled_lat + hour_num + season + (1 + scaled_yr || Binomial) + (1 | Main_researcher) + (1 | Municipality)`, restricted to records with a parseable capture time between 05:00 and 19:00. It omits longitude, elevation, moult and individual identity. The same model without `hour_num`, fitted to the identical sample, provides the comparison used to check that the year slope is unaffected by adding capture hour.

To evaluate Allen's rule [@allen1877; @ryding2021shape], which predicts that extremities enlarge in warmer conditions to facilitate non-evaporative heat dissipation, we tested whether bill width exhibited a positive temporal slope under researcher and spatial controls.

## Bivariate modeling and delta-method test of geometric isometry

To evaluate whether body shape changed over time, we analyzed the subset of records with simultaneous measurements of both wing length and body mass on the exact same individual birds ($n = 7,577$ shared records across 72 species). We fitted models estimating trait-specific decadal rates of change expressed as percentage change per decade (%/decade): $\beta_{\text{wing,\%}}$ and $\beta_{\text{mass,\%}}$.

To avoid the variance inflation induced by crossing two grouping factors that are 85.9% collinear (110 of 128 municipalities sampled by a single researcher), all models incorporated the parsimonious contributor random intercept `(1 | Main_researcher)`, alongside sex, latitude, and species-specific random slopes and intercepts across 50 phylogenetic trees.

Under geometric isometry, body mass scales with the cube of linear dimensions ($M \propto L^3$). If proportional scaling is preserved, an observed percentage change in wing length $\beta_{\text{wing,\%}}$ implies an expected percentage change in body mass of:
$$\beta_{\text{mass, expected}} = \left(1 + \frac{\beta_{\text{wing,\%}}}{100}\right)^3 - 1 \approx 3 \times \beta_{\text{wing,\%}}$$
We formally tested departure from isometry via the linear contrast:
$$\Delta_{\text{iso}} = \beta_{\text{mass,\%}} - 3 \times \beta_{\text{wing,\%}}$$
The sampling variance and standard error of $\Delta_{\text{iso}}$ were derived via the delta method:
$$\operatorname{Var}(\Delta_{\text{iso}}) = \operatorname{Var}(\beta_{\text{mass,\%}}) + 9\operatorname{Var}(\beta_{\text{wing,\%}}) - 6\operatorname{Cov}(\beta_{\text{mass,\%}}, \beta_{\text{wing,\%}})$$
$$\operatorname{SE}(\Delta_{\text{iso}}) = \sqrt{\operatorname{Var}(\Delta_{\text{iso}})}, \quad z = \frac{\Delta_{\text{iso}}}{\operatorname{SE}(\Delta_{\text{iso}})}$$
The contrast is also fitted directly as a single response ($\ln M - 3 \ln L$) under both the parsimonious and the full M3 adjustment sets, which returns its standard error exactly and removes any dependence on the covariance between two separately estimated slopes. Both routes are reported; they agree. A 95% confidence interval strictly excluding zero indicates a statistically significant departure from strict geometric isometry. A positive contrast ($\Delta_{\text{iso}} > 0$) indicates that body mass declined less than predicted by cubic scaling of the wing (mass conservation or stoutening), whereas a negative contrast ($\Delta_{\text{iso}} < 0$) indicates disproportionate mass loss or wing elongation (slenderization).

## Interannual temperature anomalies

Each capture record was linked to the mean annual temperature at its coordinates in its capture year, taken from the WorldClim historical monthly weather series (monthly tmin/tmax, 1950–2024, CRU-TS 4.09 downscaled with WorldClim 2.1, 2.5 arc-min; @harris2020crudata). This is the time-resolved product, not the WorldClim climate normals. The local annual anomaly is that value minus the locality's own mean across the sampled years ($\Delta T_{\text{local}}$). The WorldClim land mask leaves no value at 98 of the 455 coordinate localities, which lie roughly 10 km from the nearest valid cell and are not gap-filled; anomalies were therefore available for `r .n(rr_n_therm)` of the `r .n(rr_n_shared)` shared records.

We tested the association between morphology and $\Delta T_{\text{local}}$ for wing length, log body mass, the isometry contrast ($\Delta_{\text{iso}} = \ln M - 3\ln L$) and relative wing length ($\ln L - \frac{1}{3}\ln M$), fitting the same M3 adjustment set used for the temporal models (sex, latitude, longitude, elevation, season, moult; random intercepts for contributor and individual; species intercepts and anomaly slopes; phylogenetic covariance across 50 trees).

Because a temperature anomaly measured over a warming study period is itself correlated with calendar year, and because every bird caught at one locality in one year shares the same anomaly value, we ran three further specifications: calendar year and anomaly entered simultaneously; the anomaly detrended within sites; and a locality-year random intercept. All four are reported in Supplementary Note S8. We did not attempt a cluster-robust variance estimator: the random-effects structure is non-nested, which the available implementations do not support.

## Historical museum series, climate breakpoint, and sampling expansion

To contextualize the contemporary 1995–2018 window within a century-long macroecological perspective, we analyzed historical museum study skins ($n = 3,439$ adult specimens, 1884–2017) across 142 passerine species preserved in major Brazilian ornithological collections, available via the ATLANTIC BIRD TRAITS database. 

To test whether regional warming and avian morphometrics experienced structural breakpoints across the secular record, we fitted two-phase piecewise linear regressions [@muggeo2003estimating] on annual regional temperature anomalies (NASA GISS, 1880–2018) and species-centered morphological deviations:
$$y_t = \alpha + \beta_1 \min(Y_t - \tau, 0) + \beta_2 \max(Y_t - \tau, 0) + \varepsilon_t$$
where $\tau$ represents the candidate changepoint year. We fixed $\tau = 1980$ a priori, as the conventional onset of the modern warming era, and used the same year to define the pre- and post-breakpoint periods for the morphological series. This is an imposed boundary, not an estimated one, and we report it as such: a grid search over $\tau \in [1940, 1995]$ applied to the regional temperature series favours an earlier changepoint (`r rr_bp_best`, AIC `r rr_bp_best_aic`) over 1980 (AIC `r rr_bp_1980_aic`, $\Delta\text{AIC} = `r rr_bp_daic`$). The pre-1980 and post-1980 contrasts we report should therefore be read as a comparison between two a priori periods, not as evidence that the regional series breaks at 1980.

To assess the robustness of our conclusions to analytical filtering criteria, we refitted linear mixed-effects models across the broader avian community following the sampling design of @jirinec2021morphological. This expanded dataset incorporated individuals of unknown sex, all age classes, and all understorey mist-netted bird orders ($n = 46,663$ captures across 243 species; Supplementary Material), evaluating temporal slopes with random intercepts and slopes for species and random intercepts for sampling locality and contributor.

## Phenotypic variability: dispersion modeling and $\ln\text{CVR}$

Among-individual phenotypic variability was modeled using two complementary approaches. Continuous heteroscedastic dispersion models are our primary analysis, because they use the full continuous time series and adjust for covariates directly; the $\ln\text{CVR}$ meta-analysis is a complementary species-level summary that requires temporal replication within a contributor and therefore rests on a smaller, compositionally different subset.

1. **Meta-analytic $\ln\text{CVR}$** (complementary): For species with $\ge 5$ records in both the early (1995–2006) and late (2013–2018) periods, we computed the log coefficient-of-variation ratio ($\ln\text{CVR}$) with small-sample bias correction [@nakagawa2015metaanalysis]:
   $$\ln\text{CVR} = \ln\left(\frac{\operatorname{CV}_{\text{late}}}{\operatorname{CV}_{\text{early}}}\right) + \frac{1}{2(n_{\text{late}} - 1)} - \frac{1}{2(n_{\text{early}} - 1)}$$
   where sampling variance incorporates the observed correlation between log mean and log standard deviation within each period. Effect sizes were pooled in random-effects meta-analytic models using `metafor` [@viechtbauer2010metafor]. To separate variance shifts from contributor pooling, $\ln\text{CVR}$ was calculated both pooled across all contributors ($k = 54$ for wing; $k = 57$ for body mass; $k = 36$ for bill width) and strictly within the same contributor. The within-contributor version requires a species to have been sampled by the same contributor in both periods, which few combinations satisfy: it rests on `r rr_cvr_k` species $\times$ sex $\times$ contributor effect sizes drawn from `r rr_cvr_spp` species and `r rr_cvr_src` contributors (`r rr_cvr_early` early and `r rr_cvr_late` late records), all `r rr_cvr_spp` of which also appear in the pooled analysis. This is a considerably smaller and compositionally narrower subset than the pooled comparison, and it is for that reason that we treat the continuous dispersion models, which use the whole series, as the primary variance analysis.
The early and late periods are defined as $\text{Year} \le 2006$ and $\text{Year} \ge 2013$, the outer quartiles of the sampling record. The intervening years (2007–2012) are excluded by construction so that the two windows are separated in time and do not share records; they contribute to every continuous analysis, including the dispersion models below, and are omitted only from the two-period contrast.

2. **Continuous heteroscedastic dispersion models** (primary): In `glmmTMB`, we specified a dispersion submodel (`dispformula`) allowing residual standard deviation $\sigma_i$ to vary continuously over time and across contributors:
   $$\log(\sigma_i) = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 \text{scaled\_yr}_i + \alpha_2 \text{Sex}_i + u_{\text{researcher}}$$
   where $\alpha_1$ captures the decadal rate of change in residual standard deviation. In model tier S7, standardized local mean annual temperature (`scaled_tmean`) was added to the dispersion formula to test whether residual variance tracked environmental warming.

## Trophic interactions and regional prey context

Species' dietary reliance on invertebrates was extracted from the EltonTraits 1.0 database [@wilman2014eltontraits] (`Diet-Inv`, % of diet consisting of invertebrates). In continuous interaction models (Model A), `Diet-Inv` was standardized ($z$-score) and interacted with calendar year (`scaled_yr * diet_inv_std`). Wing-length trajectories were projected across the 10th (p10), 50th (p50), and 90th (p90) species-weighted percentiles of invertebrate reliance. In categorical models (Model B), diet was collapsed into Invertebrate-dominated ($\ge 50\%$ invertebrate diet) versus Other (frugivores, nectarivores, granivores, omnivores). Both models were fitted across 50 phylogenetic trees with contributor random intercepts.

As exploratory regional context only (Supplementary Note S7), we modeled litter-ant richness from the ATLANTIC ANTS database [@silva2022atlanticants] across 855 standardized field campaigns (1994–2018). We fitted negative-binomial generalized linear mixed models in `glmmTMB` specifying observed ant species richness per campaign as a function of calendar year, with the log of sampling effort (number of pitfall traps $\times$ operational days) as an offset, and random intercepts for contributor, municipality, and sampling locality.

## Reproducible software environment

Analyses and manuscript generation were conducted using R version 4.4+ with packages `glmmTMB` (v1.1.14), `prepR4pcm` (v0.1.0), `metafor` (v4.6+), `ape` (v5.8+), `sf` (v1.0+), `terra` (v1.8+), and `tidyverse` (v2.0+), alongside Python (version 3.11+) with `matplotlib` (v3.10+) and `pandas` (v2.2+). All analysis scripts, curated datasets, and fitted model objects are openly archived and fully reproducible in the project repository (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.atlantic_birds).

compilations: morphological records from ATLANTIC BIRD TRAITS

weather series (CRU-TS 4.09 downscaled; @harris2020crudata) and NASA GISTEMP v4

records. No new animal capture or handling was undertaken. Capture and ringing
permits for the primary data are those held by the contributing research
programs compiled in ATLANTIC BIRD TRAITS [@rodrigues_atlantic_2019].
